control for confounding variables in sequence analyses
sample size for rare action sequences

historical_evidence.finding: Only 2/30 stars had stable top sequential suppressors across seasons. One specific teammate sequence, Giannis Antetokounmpo → Damian Lillard DRIVE→PNR, showed a negative premium of -0.263 (n=31).

DRIVE play-type labels exhibit foul leakage: DRIVE PPP is 12pp below the foul benchmark, indicating systematic under-counting of foul-ending drives (FOUL_LEAK). OTHER possessions are inflated by foul-ending inclusion. Only 0.7% of possessions map via initiation_type.
DRIVE PPP is substantially higher in regular season (1.198) than playoffs (0.912), a -0.286 drop across 25 teams, motivating playoff adjustments.

Preceding opponent play types (e.g., PUTBACK) can suppress a star's next-possession PPP. PUTBACK was the top suppressor for 6+ stars, with d = -0.294 for D. Mitchell (n_after=95), but multiplicity was not corrected and samples were small.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Testing star-specific sequential stability across seasons and large negative premiums for teammate DRIVE→PNR pairs.
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null result overall, with only 7% of stars meeting the stability threshold, and small per-cell sample sizes (e.g., n=31) limiting inference.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Assumption that play-type PPP differences reflect true efficiency differences rather than labelling/foul artifacts.
failed_approaches.why: DRIVE labels leak foul-ending possessions, OTHER labels inflate PPP via foul endings, and initiation_type mapping captures only 0.7% of possessions, making raw play-type comparisons unreliable.

evidence_establishes: One specific drive→PNR teammate sequence (Giannis → Lillard) had a negative, not positive, PPP premium (-0.263, n=31).
DRIVE play-type labels are systematically biased by foul leakage, making any sequential analysis that depends on drive labels highly susceptible to measurement error.
Play-type PPP is sensitive to context (regular season vs playoffs) and to preceding actions, but the dominant observed effect for teammate drive→PNR is null or negative.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether, in general, a team possession labelled as a DRIVE before a PNR raises that PNR's PPP.
The sign, magnitude, or consistency of any such drive-predecessor effect across different teams, lineups, or seasons.
That the observed negative premium (Giannis→Lillard) is not an artefact of small sample size or labelling bias.
That corrected drive labels (if foul-leakage were fixed) would yield a different relationship.
own_inferences: The foul leakage documented in SF-CHT-025 implies many true drives are not recorded as DRIVE (they leak into OTHER or foul-related categories) and some possessions labelled DRIVE may be systematically different from unlabeled drives in ways that mechanistically affect subsequent PNR PPP (e.g., floor balance, transition opportunity).

If foul-ending drives are under-labelled, then the set of possessions classified as teammate DRIVE will be biased toward drives that did not end in fouls, potentially selecting for more controlled, lower-risk drives. This selection could either attenuate or reverse any true sequencing effect.

The n=31 negative premium for a single star pair, while not generalisable, suggests that any positive raise effect, if present, is unlikely to be large or robust; it is more plausible that confounders or labelling artefacts would create a spurious effect.

Any attempt to study this question with per-game play-by-play labels alone will be critically dependent on the quality of the sequence mapping from transition of possession and on the definition of 'teammate DRIVE' when possessions involve multiple actions or fouls.
uncertainties: Whether the negative premium for Giannis→Lillard would replicate in other seasons or with other stars.
The degree to which foul leakage can be corrected post-hoc without introducing new biases.
The minimal sample size required to detect a plausible effect size given the high variability of PNR PPP.
Whether the derived play-type possession records (graph database) already address or exacerbate the foul leakage problem.

historical_effect.explanation: Without historical evidence, the question might appear straightforward to test with sequence counts from the graph database. The retrieved records establish that: (a) the only prior attempt to look at teammate DRIVE→PNR found a negative, not positive, premium; and (b) the play-type labels used suffer from systematic foul leakage that undermines any drive-based analysis. These findings shift the decision from 'proceed with careful design' to 'do not proceed until measurement reliability is resolved'.

blocking_constraints.text: DRIVE labels are known to exhibit foul leakage and under-represent foul-ending drives (SF-CHT-025), so any exposure variable based on these labels is substantially misclassified.
Teammate drive immediately before a PNR (within the same stint/quarter) may be a rare event, and per-pair counts from SF-APPA-058 were as low as n=31, threatening power and stability.
Game context (score, period, lineup, opponent defense, substitution patterns, transition vs half-court) strongly affects both the probability of a drive and the efficiency of a subsequent PNR.

prior_work.summary: Prior project research has directly examined one DRIVE→PNR teammate pair and found a negative premium (Giannis→Lillard, -0.263, n=31). It also discovered systematic foul leakage in DRIVE labelling and established that play-type PPP is context-dependent. No prior study has attempted the general hypothesis that any teammate DRIVE raises PNR PPP, but the existing evidence collectively indicates substantial measurement and inference barriers.

risks.text: DRIVE labels are contaminated by foul leakage: an unknown fraction of true drives are missed or misclassified, and the criteria for labelling a possession as DRIVE may correlate with its outcome, biasing any sequence comparison.

Numerous game-state and lineup confounders (score margin, remaining time, possession shot clock, defensive scheme, rest days) could produce spurious associations between a preceding drive and PNR efficiency.
The combination of requiring a teammate DRIVE and a following PNR by the same team may yield sparse cell counts, as seen in SF-APPA-058, making estimates noisy and sensitive to outliers.

If play-type labels are derived using post-hoc classification that considers the outcome of the possession (e.g., points scored), the label 'DRIVE' may be applied differently to successful and unsuccessful possessions, introducing look-ahead bias.
Testing across many possible pairings or possession intervals would require pre-specified adjustment to avoid inflated false-positive rates.
Playing style and play-type definitions may evolve across seasons, threatening the stability of any estimated effect when pooling 2022-23 through 2025-26 data.

design.estimand: The average difference in PNR PPP (points scored directly from the PNR action divided by the number of PNR possessions) when the immediately preceding team possession was a DRIVE, minus the average PNR PPP when the preceding possession was any other non-DRIVE action, within the same lineup stint and controlling for game context.
design.unit: A team possession (offensive trip down the floor until a shot, turnover, or foul ends the possession).
design.sample: All regular-season and playoff possessions from 2022-23 through 2025-26 where the offensive team runs a PNR, excluding overtime and possessions with a preceding time-out or inter-period gap, and retaining only possessions where the preceding possession can be unambiguously linked to the same team and same stint.
design.power: Cannot be assessed without a reliable drive label. Even with large N, measurement error in DRIVE will attenuate effect sizes and reduce effective power. A formal power analysis would require an effect size estimate from validated labels; the single available estimate is -0.263 with n=31, suggesting any positive effect is small at best.
design.controls: Game period and score margin at start of possession, shot clock at start of possession (if available), home/away, starting vs bench lineup indicator, opponent defensive rating percentile, and an interaction with regular season/playoffs.
design.falsification: 1) Test for balance on observable pre-treatment characteristics (e.g., shot clock, score margin, opponent defensive strength) between drive-preceded and non-drive-preceded PNR possessions. 2) Verify that the sequence labelling (preceding possession is a drive by any teammate) does not predict game outcomes or other future events beyond the immediate PNR, implying no look-ahead leakage. 3) Reproduce the known foul leakage pattern for DRIVE possessions in the analysis sample to confirm the measurement problem is present.
design.multiplicity: A single pre-registered hypothesis test on the pooled sample, with a pre-specified subgroup analysis by team if sample permits, using Holm-Bonferroni correction for the number of team subgroups tested.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null at α=0.05 if the adjusted p-value for the ATE of teammate DRIVE on PNR PPP is <0.05 AND the falsification checks pass. If the falsification checks reveal substantial imbalance or label leakage, the result will be considered invalid regardless of p-value.
design.data_version: 2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons from per-game play-by-play, with the graph-derived play-type possession records. However, this design is not executable with current data because SF-CHT-025 demonstrated that DRIVE labels are not sufficiently reliable. The minimum viable version would require externally validated or corrected drive labels (e.g., from manual annotation or tracking data) before the sequence analysis can be trusted.

You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.

1. Read the research objective and the data description.

The research question: "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP." This is in the area of play-type labeling and data quality.

Data available: multiple seasons of NBA data, including play-by-play, rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchups, box-score summary, and derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from play-by-play.

We need to break down the question: "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP." This means: if a teammate (not the initiator of the pick-and-roll) had a DRIVE action preceding that PNR possession, does that increase the points per possession (PPP) of the PNR? So we're looking at sequences of offensive actions: a drive by one player, then later in the same possession (or perhaps within some time window) a pick-and-roll by another player, and whether that sequence leads to higher efficiency for the PNR.

Thus, research concepts likely involve:
- Play types: DRIVE, PNR (pick-and-roll), maybe other actions.
- Sequential dependency: preceding action (drive) affecting efficiency of subsequent action (PNR).
- Teammate interaction: not the same player.
- Points per possession (PPP) as outcome.
- Defensive adjustments: maybe defense is scrambled after a drive, leading to better PNR outcomes.

Methodological questions:
- How to define "teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR"? What time window? Within the same possession? The same shot clock? Need to operationalize "preceding". Does "preceding" mean immediately before in the same possession, or within some number of actions? 
- How to attribute points to the PNR specifically when multiple actions occur? The derived play-type possession records likely label a possession with a primary play type, but if a drive occurs before the PNR, is the possession tagged as PNR? The graph database may allow linking actions within a possession.
- Risk of confounding: maybe drives are more likely to precede PNRs in certain game contexts (e.g., when the defense is already in rotation, or when the shot clock is low), which could independently affect PNR efficiency.
- Data quality: labeling of play types (DRIVE, PNR) from play-by-play data may be noisy. How reliable are these labels? Is the derived play-type possession record capturing the right play type? Could be misclassification.
- Sample size and power: how many possessions have a teammate drive preceding a PNR? Might be sparse.
- Selection bias: not all drives are followed by a PNR; selection into the sequence might be related to defensive reaction.
- Multiple testing if many similar hypotheses are tested.
- Leakage/lookahead: if we use future information to label drives or PNRs, but likely not.
- Mechanical floor/ceiling effects: PPP is bounded.

So concepts: "DRIVE play type", "PNR play type", "teammate interaction", "preceding action", "possession sequencing", "points per possession", "play-type labeling reliability", "confounding by game context", "sparsity of sequences".

Methodological questions: "operational definition of preceding", "attribution of points in multi-action possessions", "reliability and validity of play-type labels from play-by-play", "confounding control", "sample size for rare sequence", "selection bias from possession flow".

We'll now construct a query.

Call retrieve_history.

We are in stage 2. We received retrieval results with four study families: SF-APPA-058, SF-CHT-025, SF-APPS-011, SF-APPA-050. Now I need to use this evidence to assess the current research question: "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP." I need to see if any of these records directly address this question or provide relevant evidence. Let's examine each:

- FAM:SF-APPA-058: About season stability of top suppressors and negative teammate pairs. It mentions a negative pair: "Giannis->Lillard DRIVE->PNR -0.263 n=31". That's directly relevant: it's a specific teammate drive preceding a PNR, and the effect on PNR PPP (or probably the premium) is negative -0.263 with n=31. The outcome status is "rejected" (the hypothesis was about stability, but it found only a few stable suppressors; but the specific finding of a negative premium might be relevant). The failure mechanism is "B_powered_null" and limited by "LIM:small_sample". So this earlier study observed a drive->PNR sequence for one star pair (Giannis to Lillard) and found a negative effect, not a positive one. But it's a single case, not a general test.

- FAM:SF-CHT-025: Play-type labeling audit: OTHER/DRIVE foul leakage. It found artifacts in play-type labeling, specifically that DRIVE has foul leakage and OTHER has inflated PPP due to foul endings. This is highly relevant to the question's measurement reliability: if DRIVE labels are unreliable (foul leakage, misclassification), then identifying a preceding DRIVE might be noisy, and any PPP calculation could be biased. This is an artifact finding. It says "Play-type PPP differences are real efficiency, not labeling/foul artifacts." The result showed OTHER inflated, DRIVE 12pp below foul benchmark, PNR 22% foul rate. So this suggests that play-type labeling has systematic errors. This could confound any attempt to study drive->PNR sequences, because the labeling of the drive itself might be flawed, and the PNR PPP might be affected by fouls.

- FAM:SF-APPS-011: Regular season vs playoff PPP by play type (DRIVE over-prediction). This shows DRIVE PPP differs by context (RS vs playoffs). It might be relevant to the need to control for context or season type when comparing sequences, but not directly about preceding drive.

- FAM:SF-APPA-050: Superstar sequential suppression: opponent play before the star. This is about opponent's preceding play type affecting star's next-possession PPP. Not directly about teammate drive, but about sequential effects. It shows that specific preceding play types can affect PPP. This establishes the existence of sequential effects, though from opponent side.

So, the most directly relevant is SF-APPA-058 with a specific pair drive->PNR negative premium, but with small sample and not a general question. The labeling audit SF-CHT-025 highlights serious labeling issues for DRIVE. These two are key.

I need to compile historical_evidence and failed_approaches lists from these retrieved records exactly as they are. The record statuses: SF-APPA-058: "rejected"; SF-CHT-025: "artifact"; SF-APPS-011: "supported"; SF-APPA-050: "not a hypothesis test". But I can include all as historical_evidence because they are relevant to the research concepts or methodological questions. The failed_approaches would highlight approaches that failed and why, as recorded. SF-APPA-058 is a failed approach because it only looked at stability and had small sample for specific pairs; it failed to find many stable suppressors. SF-CHT-025 is an artifact finding, so that could be a failed approach in that the hypothesis that play-type PPP differences are real was found to be an artifact. I should list the failed approaches as recorded.

Now, I need to complete steps 4-9. Let's summarize: historical findings: the labeling audit reveals DRIVE foul leakage and OTHER inflated PPP; the sequential suppression study found specific teammate drive->PNR negative effect (Giannis->Lillard) but n=31 and limited stability; overall, no general test of the question exists. Evidence establishes that play-type labels have systematic biases, especially for DRIVE, and that one specific pair had a negative effect, not positive. It does not establish that a teammate drive generally raises PNR PPP; it suggests the opposite for one pair, and that labeling issues could make such analysis unreliable.

I need to make my own inferences and identify uncertainties. For example: from SF-CHT-025, if DRIVE is often misclassified (foul leakage), then counting "preceding DRIVE" might be biased, especially if the foul ending causes the possession to be mislabeled or if a drive that ends in a foul is not recorded as a drive. This could create a mechanical floor: PNR PPP might appear higher after drives simply because drives that don't end in fouls are undercounted, or something. There is also a risk of outcome-derived label: the labeling of a possession as DRIVE might depend on its outcome (points, foul). So any sequence analysis could be artifact-driven.

Testability: Given the labeling uncertainty and the small sample needed for specific teammate sequences (you need a player to drive, then the same team gets possession back (teammate?), wait: "Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR" - the question is: if any teammate has a drive possession, then the next possession for that same team is a PNR, does the PNR have higher PPP? The unit might be team possessions. The data covers several seasons, so there should be many possessions where a team had a drive then a PNR. But the labeling of DRIVE is unreliable (SF-CHT-025). Also, we need to define "preceding" - same quarter? same game? The data likely allows linking consecutive team possessions. But there are many confounding variables: time in game, score, opponent, lineup, possession type availability, etc. The sample size might be large enough, but the effect might be small and confounded. The existence of one pair with negative effect (n=31) suggests that the effect might be negative, but not stable. So I'd assess testability as moderate probability, say 0.4, because of labeling issues and confounding. Predicted outcome: I think a competent test might find an artifact or be inconclusive due to labeling issues, so artifact probability high, rejected possibility if null, etc. I'd put supported low, artifact high, uncertain moderate.

Decision: Probably do_not_proceed because of the unreliable DRIVE labeling. Or proceed_with_changes: first need to validate play-type labeling for drives and ensure accurate labeling before such a sequence analysis. But as the task is to decide before any analysis, I can recommend do_not_proceed, with design suggestions for a minimal viable test that would address labeling first.

I need to fill the schema. I'll include the retrieved records in historical_evidence: all four because they touch on concepts, but I'll focus evidence_establishes and does_not_establish on the relevant ones. I'll cite SF-APPA-058 and SF-CHT-025 heavily.

Design: even if do_not_proceed, I need to propose a design. If labeling cannot be trusted, a pre-registered test would need to first define a reliable drive label, perhaps using optical tracking or manual annotation, not the current derived labels. So I might still describe the estimand: difference in PNR PPP when the preceding team possession was a drive vs not a drive, controlling for lineup, score, etc. But I can state that with current data the labeling risk is too high.

Now, I'll write the JSON. Start with research_concepts and methodological_questions from retrieval call, maybe refined. Then historical_evidence array with each record. Then failed_approaches: SF-APPA-058 failed due to small sample and null result for stability; SF-CHT-025 is an artifact finding so approach of using raw play-type labels for PPP differences failed. I'll list them.

Then evidence_establishes: that one specific drive->PNR pair had a negative premium; that DRIVE play-type labels have systematic foul leakage; that other sequential suppression effects exist but are small and unstable. Evidence_does_not_establish: general effect of teammate drive on PNR PPP, direction or magnitude, and whether labeling artifacts would bias any observed effect.

Own_inferences: e.g., the DRIVE foul leakage likely means many true drives are not labeled as DRIVE if they end in fouls, or vice versa; this could create a mechanical relationship where a PNR after a "drive" might have different foul rates, affecting PPP. The negative finding for Giannis->Lillard (n=31) suggests the hypothesis of a positive raise is unlikely. Uncertainties: whether labeling bias could flip the sign, sample size needed.

Historical_effect: yes changed_decision because prior work shows labeling unreliability and a specific negative finding, so proceeding without addressing labeling would be high risk. So changed_decision: yes.

Testability: p_testable=0.3 maybe, given the risks. Blocking constraints: MEASURE_RELIABILITY, SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER? For rare sequences, possibly SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, but I'll pick MEASURE_RELIABILITY as main.

Prior_work: already_answered: partly, cited: ["FAM:SF-APPA-058", "FAM:SF-CHT-025", "FAM:SF-APPS-011", "FAM:SF-APPA-050"]. Summary: "Earlier work found a specific negative teammaterome drive-PNR premium and uncovered systematic foul leakage in DRIVE labeling, making any drive-based analysis suspect."

Risks: list codes and texts: MEASURE_RELIABILITY: DRIVE play-type labels exhibit foul leakage (SF-CHT-025); CONFOUNDING: many game-context variables; EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: specific teammate sequences may be rare; LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD: derived labels might use future results.

Predicted_outcome: supported 0.1, rejected 0.2, untestable 0.3, artifact 0.3, uncertain 0.1.

Decision: do_not_proceed. Design: describe a minimal viable test that would require validated drive labels, etc.
